newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia says toll from fatal virus stabilised.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says toll from fatal virus stabilised.

text.p: The death toll from an airborne virus that has killed at least 26 small children and baffled international medical experts has stabilised, Malaysia's health minister said.
A lethal strain of what Malaysian health officials say is Coxsackie virus had claimed no fatalities in almost two weeks, Health Minister Chua Jui Meng said on Sunday.
"I am happy with the situation," the national news agency Bernama quoted Chua as saying.

The outbreak of Coxsackie has caused hundreds of cases of the relatively benign foot-and-mouth disease but has also led to myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart muscle, and the child fatalities, almost all of them under the age of four.
As of Saturday, 1,240 children had been admitted to hospitals throughout the country for suspected Coxsackie B and A infection and 968 had been discharged, Chua said.
Health authorities have advised parents throughout the country to keep small children indoors, despite the fact that all of the myocarditis cases have struck in Malaysia's Borneo state of Sarawak.

Malaysia called in experts from Atlanta's Centres for Disease Control and Prevention earlier this month. They found traces of another virus in at least two of the victims that has no known cure or vaccine, Health ministry officials said.
Medical authorities have exchanged opinions about the virus on the Internet and the University of Nebraska Medical Centre in the United States has a web site tracking developments about the disease.
"...the identity of the virus -- if it is a virus -- that has caused the pediatric deaths remains a mystery...," the centre said in an update last week.
A lively newsgroup page has appeared on the Internet featuring scorching criticisms of how Malaysian health authorities are handling the outbreak along with oddball theories on how to cure it.
Chua last week angered parents in Peninsular Malaysia for not doing enough to keep their children indoors, although there have been no fatalities thus far in the peninsula.

"There is an element of complacency among parents (in the peninsula) and they think the outbreak (in Sarawak) does not concern them," he told reporters. "Parents have to isolate them from public places."
What has puzzled health officials is why the virus is killing children in Sarawak and nowhere else in Malaysia.
